161.quote_or_event: “Benevolence (maitrī) towards all living-beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion and sympathy (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and tolerance (mādhyasthya) towards the insolent and ill-behaved (avineya) are the other observances.”
161.explanation: Umāsvāti names four standing attitudes a vow-holder must cultivate, and the second, pramoda, is gladness at another's excellence, which is the exact inner opposite of envy; Pūjyapāda's commentary glosses it as fervent affection and veneration in the presence of the virtuous.
161.tie_back: Valluvar asks that an envy-free heart be adopted as the very rule of conduct, and the Tattvārtha makes joy at others' virtue a fixed observance (bhāvanā) that supports every vow.
161.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 7.11, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
161._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; pramoda is Jainism's own named virtue of rejoicing in others' merit, a strong fit for the inner rule against envy, though the sutra frames it among several observances, not as envy's opposite alone.

162.quote_or_event: “I forgive all living beings and may all living beings forgive me; I cherish feelings of friendship towards all and I harbour enmity towards none.”
162.explanation: This is the Prakrit formula (khāmemi savva jīve) recited at the annual Paryuṣaṇa confession, in which the Jain declares friendship with every being and ill-will towards none.
162.tie_back: Valluvar prizes freedom from envy towards anyone at all (yār māṭṭum) above every other gain, and the Jain formula likewise refuses any exception: friendship towards all, enmity towards none.
162.source: Saman Suttam, verse 86 (English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
162._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim in the Saman Suttam English text on jainworld.com; the universal scope matches the kural closely, but the verse speaks of enmity and forgiveness rather than envy specifically, and does not rank it above all other gains.

163.quote_or_event: “Spite against knowledge–pradoṣa, concealment of knowledge–nihnava, non-imparting of knowledge out of envy–mātsarya, causing impediment to acquisition of knowledge–antarāya, disregard of knowledge–āsādana, and disparagement of true knowledge–upaghāta, lead to the influx (āsrava) of knowledge-obscuring (jñānāvaraṇa) and faith-obscuring (darśanāvaraṇa) karmas.”
163.explanation: In Jain karma theory envy (mātsarya) and spite towards another's learning do not harm the other person; they draw in karmic matter that clouds the envier's own knowledge and faith.
163.tie_back: Valluvar says the man who envies another's prosperity in effect wants neither virtue nor prosperity for himself, and the Tattvārtha shows the mechanism: envy blocks the envier's own spiritual growth.
163.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.10, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
163._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; the sutra explicitly names envy as self-harming, but its envy is about withholding knowledge, not resenting another's prosperity, so the fit is partial.

164.quote_or_event: “The two sins attachment and aversion lead one to commit sinful acts. That monk who always besieges them will not wander in this mundane existence.”
164.explanation: Jainism traces all wrongdoing to the twin passions of rāga (attachment) and dveṣa (aversion), and teaches that one who sees this and checks them escapes the round of suffering in saṃsāra.
164.tie_back: Valluvar's wise man refuses to do wrong out of envy because he knows the suffering it leads to, and the Jain verse likewise sees aversion, of which envy is a form, as the root of sinful acts whose fruit is continued wandering in suffering.
164.source: Saman Suttam, verse 130 (Samyamasutra; English tr. T.K. Tukol and K.K. Dixit; jainworld.com)
164._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on jainworld.com's Saman Suttam page; a reasonable fit on knowing where passion leads, but the verse addresses monks and attachment/aversion generally rather than envy by name.

165.quote_or_event: The god Saṅgamaka, hearing Śakra praise Mahāvīra's steadfastness, set out to break him: “His jealousy increased greatly when he saw Śrī Vīra standing so, undisturbed, a disinterested friend of the world.” After six months of failed torments he lamented, “how long have I wandered over the earth, alas! deceived by my own stupidity!”
165.explanation: Hemacandra's account has the envious god throw every terror at Mahāvīra without disturbing his meditation, while Saṅgamaka himself breaks his vow, loses his radiance and is expelled from heaven.
165.tie_back: Valluvar says envy alone suffices to ruin the envier even if his foes do him no harm, and Saṅgamaka's jealousy left its target untouched while destroying Saṅgamaka himself.
165.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X (Mahāvīracaritra), ch. IV, Part 4 “Attacks by Saṅgamaka” (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)
165._accuracy_note: Both sentences verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; the story names jealousy explicitly and shows it ruining the jealous party while the envied one is unharmed, a near-direct narrative fit.

166.quote_or_event: “Laying obstacles (vighna) (in way of charity, etc.) is the cause of the influx of obstructive (antarāya) karmas.”
166.explanation: Jain doctrine holds that obstructing another's giving, gain or enjoyment binds antarāya karma, which in turn obstructs the obstructer's own future charity, gain, and enjoyment of food, clothing and other goods.
166.tie_back: Valluvar warns that one who resents what is given to others will end without food or clothing, and the Tattvārtha's karma law says the same: blocking another's gift blocks one's own receiving.
166.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.27, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
166._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (the Hindi gloss lists obstruction of charity, gain, enjoyment and consumables); a strong doctrinal parallel to resenting gifts, though the kural's ruin of the kin is not addressed.

167.quote_or_event: When the envious god Saṅgamaka returned to heaven after failing to shake Mahāvīra, Śakra at once turned his back on him and declared him unfit to be seen; Saṅgamaka, his beauty blurred like a mirror sprinkled with water, was expelled from the Saudharma heaven.
167.explanation: In Hemacandra's telling the envious god loses his splendour and his place among the gods, and the king of gods publicly turns away from him and casts him out.
167.tie_back: Valluvar pictures Fortune turning from the envious man and pointing him out to Misfortune, and the nearest Jain image is Śakra turning his back on the envious Saṅgamaka and driving him from heaven's prosperity.
167.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X, ch. IV, Part 4 “Attacks by Saṅgamaka” (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)
167._accuracy_note: Paraphrase checked against the wisdomlib.org text; Jainism has no goddesses of fortune and misfortune who judge people (results follow from karma), so this is a next-best narrative echo of the image, and it reuses the Saṅgamaka story from kural 165.

168.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
168.explanation: The young ascetic who calls himself “without a protector” tells King Śreṇika that the worst enemy a person can have is his own perverted disposition, which brings him to grief at death and, as the preceding verses say, to hell.
168.tie_back: Valluvar personifies envy as a sinner without equal that wrecks a man's wealth and drives him to the fire of hell, and the Jain verse likewise ranks the inner vice above any outward foe as the agent of ruin.
168._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the inner-vice-as-worst-enemy idea fits well, but the verse is about a lax monk's perversity in general, not envy specifically (Jacobi also notes vv. 38-53 are likely a later addition).

169.quote_or_event: When Mahāvīra broke his fast at the proud, wealthy Abhinava's house, a stream of treasure fell there, while the devout but ruined Jinadatta, who had waited in vain, gained nothing visible; an omniscient disciple of Pārśva then explained that Jinadatta had earned rebirth in the Acyuta heaven, and that “the stream of treasure, fruit in this world of the Arhat’s fast-breaking was obtained by Sheth Abhinava, who is devoid of pure character.”
169.explanation: The episode answers why a man of poor character can prosper while a good man stays poor: visible wealth is only a this-worldly fruit, and the real merit lies with the pure-minded, to bear fruit in time.
169.tie_back: Valluvar says the prosperity of the envious and the poverty of the upright must be pondered, and this Jain story ponders exactly that case and resolves it through karma and inner disposition.
169.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book X, ch. IV, Part 4 (episode of Jīrṇaśreṣṭhin and Abhinava) (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS)
169._accuracy_note: Quoted sentence verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org (the surrounding narrative is paraphrased); a strong fit for the puzzle of the bad prospering and the good suffering, though Abhinava's fault is pride and deceit rather than envy.

170.quote_or_event: “Censuring others, praising oneself, concealing good qualities present in others and proclaiming noble qualities absent in oneself, cause the influx (āsrava) of karmas which lead to low-status (nīcagotra).”
170.explanation: Jain karma theory holds that belittling others and hiding their merits, the habits of the envious, bind karma that brings low standing in future lives, while the next sutra (6.26) assigns high standing to the reverse disposition.
170.tie_back: Valluvar concludes that no one ever grew great through envy, and the Tattvārtha makes it a law of karma that the envious habit of concealing others' virtues leads downward, never up.
170.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 6.25, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018)
170._accuracy_note: 6.25 verified verbatim on wisdomlib.org; 6.26 is described, not quoted. A good fit for envy-like conduct leading to decline, but the sutra concerns status (gotra) in future births, not worldly prosperity.
